# ChainWatch model card

Scope: the transaction-scoring model and the rule ensemble behind `chainwatch.detector`.
Card version tracks `configs/default.toml`; retraining (`make models` / `make calibrate`)
regenerates every artefact named here, and the numbers below are rendered from
`results/summary.json` by `make report`.

## What the model is

- Trained detector variants B0 (single payment), B1 (account history) and G2 (graph
  features), each a gradient-boosted tree ensemble exported to portable JSON and evaluated by
  a pure-Python tree walker (architecture in `docs/architecture.md`).
- Rule ensemble: 13 hard rules whose evidence score feeds the ring matcher.
- Input: 59 detection features per payment event, generated by one streaming
  implementation for both training replay and serving; feature set prioritised as
  {{ cfg.features.priority | raw }}. No account identifiers, no PII fields.
- Export budget: at most {{ cfg.model.ship_max_trees | int }} trees per model, depth
  {{ cfg.model.max_depth | int }}.
- Ring matcher: at least {{ cfg.rings.min_accounts | int }} accounts and
  {{ cfg.rings.min_flagged_edges | int }} flagged edges per ring, flagged edges linked within
  {{ cfg.rings.link_window_s | int }} s; a ring is caught when
  {{ cfg.eval.catch_min_accounts | int }} of its accounts carry at least a
  {{ cfg.eval.catch_min_action | raw }} tier action.
- Output: an event score, a rule hit, and — after ring linking — a ring-level alert with
  hop path and evidence.

## Intended use

- Offline evaluation and red-teaming of mule-detection logic against simulated payment
  worlds, and as a reference implementation for how a ring-level alerting pipeline is
  scored honestly (pre-registered expectations, leakage battery, paired baselines).
- Research/educational use on ChainWorld and other labelled or synthetic datasets the user
  generates themselves.

## Out-of-scope use

- No production alerting, no real-customer scoring, no compliance or law-enforcement
  decisions. The repo has never seen a real bank ledger; the PaySim profile is unlabelled
  and supports distribution sanity checks only.
- No claim of accuracy, savings or parity against any published system: we do not claim
  parity with MuleHunter or others, and we have not compared implementations, datasets or
  thresholds.
- Thresholds calibrated on ChainWorld FPR targets are not transferable; any local use must
  recalibrate on local validation data (see retrain below).

## Ethics and data protection

- Training/evaluation data is fully synthetic (ChainWorld) or public and unlabelled
  (PaySim); no personal data is processed or distributed by this repo.
- The feature set deliberately excludes identity attributes, so the model cannot be used to
  profile demographic groups; its outputs describe transaction patterns, not people.
- Failure costs are asymmetric by design: the operating point targets a low false-alarm
  rate because false accusations of money-mule activity can harm legitimate account
  holders; the report publishes the realised false-alarm rates per archetype for exactly
  this reason.

## Retraining and reproduction

```bash
make models PRESET=medium    # features, train, thresholds, verify the model package
make calibrate               # world difficulty check with B0 and B1 only (never G2)
make eval-all                # re-run the protocol, regenerate summary/ablation/robustness/leakage
make report                  # re-render this card's numbers into docs/model_card.md
make check-claims            # verify every rendered number against results/
```

Retrain triggers: any change to the config (`configs/default.toml`, the world presets, the
feature flags file), or the feature code; also re-run when the leakage battery or a
pre-registered expectation fails — a failed expectation invalidates the card until
explained in `reports/REPORT.md`.
